name: Soviet Union

areaKm2.note: world_1960 USSR polygon = ~21.74M km2 computed on the sphere (low). Official USSR area 22,402,200 km2 (mid/high).

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1989 = 287,630k (mid). OWID population CSV USSR 1989 = 289.12M (high). January 1989 census ~286.7M (low, from memory).

urbanization.note: Population-weighted OWID urban share of the 15 union republics in 1989 = 65.7% (OWID population and urban CSVs; Russia 73.4%). Low = COW upop/tpop = 113.5M/287.6M = 0.39 (cities over 100,000 only).

activePersonnel.note: COW NMC v7 milper 1989 = 3,700k (low). Soviet Armed Forces article infobox: 4.9M active in 1985. Soviet official figure published early 1989 ~4.26M (high, from memory), before the 500,000 unilateral cut announced Dec 1988 (Odom via Soviet Armed Forces article). Excludes KGB border troops and MVD internal troops.

trainedReserves.note: Soviet Army infobox: 4,129,506 reserve (1991) (low). Western estimates of reservists with service in the last five years ~5-6M; the total reserve obligation was far larger (~55M). Callable in ~30 days counted only.

supportPersonnel.note: Active minus P roles: Strategic Rocket Forces, Air Defence Forces, Air Forces, Navy (~450k), rear services and construction troops, plus Ground Forces tank, artillery, air defence and support arms (4.0M - ~750k infantry).

mobilizationRatio.note: Krivosheev, Soviet Casualties and Combat Losses (1997), ch. 2: ~34.5M mobilized 1941-45 from ~196M pre-war population (~0.18). Mid 0.15 for an older, more urban 1989 population; high 0.2. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Motor-rifle infantry of ~150 motor-rifle divisions (SMP 1989 counts 132 active MRDs), most at reduced or cadre strength; Ground Forces had nearly two million men (SMP 1989; Zickel and Keefe 1991 p. 705 via Soviet Army article). Infantry about a third of ground strength.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: BMP-2, AK-74, RPG-18/22; Category A divisions modern, cadre divisions older kit

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: two-year conscripts, little NCO corps, dedovshchina; Category B/C divisions low readiness

count.note: VDV (7 airborne divisions ~60,000), air-assault brigades (~20,000), Naval Infantry 18,000 in 1989 (Soviet Navy article) and Spetsnaz brigades.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: BMD air-droppable IFVs, Mi-8 assault lift

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: elite VDV and Spetsnaz, Afghanistan combat experience

count.note: Soviet Military Power 1989: 49,000 artillery pieces, mortars and MRLs of 100 mm or larger. IISS Military Balance 1991-92 (via Soviet Army article): 33,000 towed, ~9,000 SP and 8,000 MRL in 1991.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: 2S1/2S3/2S5/2S19, BM-27 and BM-30 MRLs; massed rather than precise fires

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: artillery the elite arm of the Soviet army, but conscript gunners

count.note: Soviet Military Power 1989 (DoD), ground forces equipment: over 53,000 main battle tanks before the announced reductions. IISS Military Balance 1991-92 p. 37 (via Soviet Army article): ~54,400 MBTs on 1 June 1991 (5,400 T-80, 9,000 T-72, 4,900 T-64, 8,500 T-62, 10,600 T-54/55, 16,000 in store east of the Urals) plus ~1,000 PT-76.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: T-80/T-72/T-64 with composite armour and Kontakt ERA, but ~40% are T-54/55/T-62 a generation behind

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript crews, limited live firing

count.note: Soviet Military Power 1989: 61,000 APC/IFVs. IISS Military Balance 1991-92 p. 37 (via Soviet Army article): over 50,000 APCs plus ~28,000 AIFVs in 1991 (high).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: BMP-2 and BTR-80 modern, BTR-60/BMP-1 older

count.note: Soviet Air Forces article, inventory 1990: 1,275 fighters (50 MiG-21, 595 MiG-23, 90 Su-27, 540 MiG-29); Soviet Air Defence Forces article, IISS Military Balance 1991-92 p. 38: 2,370 PVO interceptors (500 Su-15, 890 MiG-23, 480 MiG-25, 230 Su-27, 270 MiG-31). Total 3,645. SMP 1989 gives 5,970 tactical aircraft in all roles.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: MiG-29, Su-27, MiG-31 entering; MiG-23/Su-15 dated, weaker avionics than F-15

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: rigid GCI-controlled tactics, fewer flight hours than NATO

count.note: Soviet Air Forces article, inventory 1990: 175 strategic bombers (160 Tu-95, 15 Tu-160), 390 medium bombers (Tu-16, Tu-22, Tu-22M), 2,510 attack aircraft (Su-17, Su-24, Su-25, MiG-27) = 3,075; plus Soviet Naval Aviation strike aircraft (SMP 1989: 160 Backfire in SNA, ~175 SNA Badgers) partly overlapping.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Su-24, Tu-22M3, Tu-160 modern; few precision weapons

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Afghanistan close-support experience, limited flight hours

count.note: Soviet Military Power 1989: 4,300 ground forces helicopters. IISS Military Balance 1991-92 (via Soviet Army article): ~4,500 helicopters in 1991 incl. ~2,050 armed (1,420 Mi-24). Mid adds naval helicopters.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Mi-24 and Mi-8 robust; Mi-28/Ka-50 not yet in service

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: extensive Afghanistan combat experience

count.note: Educated guess: Tu-143 Reys and Tu-141 Strizh reconnaissance UAVs (Group 4/5) with Frontal Aviation and Ground Forces recce units; ~950 Tu-143 built 1973-89.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: film-camera recon drones, recovered by parachute

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: specialist units

count.note: Soviet Navy infobox (1990): 5 aircraft carriers (Kiev class, Kuznetsov), 2 helicopter carriers, 3 battlecruisers (Kirov), 30 cruisers, 45 destroyers, 113 frigates = 198. 1989 slightly higher (older ships not yet retired).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Kirov, Slava, Sovremenny, Udaloy modern; no CATOBAR carrier

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: low sea time, conscript crews

count.note: Soviet Navy infobox (1990): 124 corvettes, 425 patrol boats, 35 amphibious warfare ships = 584; high adds ~300 mine-warfare ships (SMP 1989 lists MCM squadrons per fleet).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Tarantul, Nanuchka missile corvettes

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript crews

count.note: Soviet Navy infobox (1990): 63 SSBN, 72 cruise-missile, 68 nuclear attack, 63 conventional attack = 266 plus 9 auxiliary. Mid-1989 somewhat higher before 1990 retirements (high).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Akula, Sierra, Typhoon, Delta IV, Oscar II modern; many noisy older boats

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: long-service officers, conscript ratings

count.note: Launchers: >1,400 ICBMs in 1989 (Strategic Rocket Forces article, citing the Library of Congress Soviet Union country study) plus 1,460 ground forces SSM launchers (FROG, SS-21, Scud) in Soviet Military Power 1989. Remaining SS-20 launchers (over half eliminated by mid-1989 under the INF Treaty per the SRF article) add 0-300. SLBM tubes are in submarines.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: SS-18 heavy MIRVed ICBM, mobile SS-24 and SS-25, accurate SS-21

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: Strategic Rocket Forces the elite service

count.note: Batteries. Ground forces: 4,900 SAM launchers (SMP 1989) at ~4 per battery = ~1,200; PVO strategic SAMs ~8,000 launchers (SMP 1989; 1990 list in the PVO article: 1,400 S-25, 2,400 S-75, 1,000 S-125, 1,950 S-200, 1,700 S-300) at ~6 per site = ~1,350; 12,000 AAA guns (SMP 1989; Zickel and Keefe p. 708) at ~6 per battery = ~2,000.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: S-300P/V, Buk, Tor: the densest and among the best integrated air defences of 1989

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Mathias Rust landed in Red Square in May 1987

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: General Staff academy system, operational-art doctrine (deep operations, OMGs); centralised command, Afghanistan exposed weak junior leadership

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: national conscript army split along ethnic lines (Slav vs Central Asian/Caucasian conscripts), dedovshchina hazing, 1989 nationalist unrest in the Baltics and Caucasus

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.25-0.5. Evidence: withdrawal from Afghanistan completed Feb 1989, glasnost criticism of the army, unilateral cuts and housing shortages

weapons.note: Anchor: weapons 9 (1985). Evidence: T-80U, BMP-2, 2S19, SS-21, Kh-29/Kh-25 guided missiles; fewer precision munitions than NATO

armor.note: Anchor: armor 9 (composite armour). Evidence: T-64B/T-72B/T-80 composite with Kontakt-1 and Kontakt-5 ERA; most tanks older types

ships.note: Anchor: ships 9 (nuclear subs, Aegis). Evidence: nuclear submarines, Kirov battlecruisers, no Aegis-equivalent until later; first conventional-takeoff carrier Kuznetsov on trials 1989

fortification.note: Anchor: fortification 9 (hardened shelters). Evidence: hardened ICBM silos and command bunkers, hardened aircraft shelters

logistics.note: Anchor: logistics between 8 (motor transport, rail) and 9. Evidence: rail-centric operational logistics, large truck parks, An-124/Il-76 airlift, limited containerisation

communications.note: Anchor: communications between 8 and 9. Evidence: Molniya and Raduga satellite comms at strategic level; tactical radios analogue, limited data links

isr.note: Anchor: isr 9 (satellites). Evidence: Zenit/Yantar imaging and US-A RORSAT ocean surveillance satellites, A-50 AWACS (15 aircraft)

air.note: Anchor: air 9 (1985). Evidence: MiG-29, Su-27, MiG-31, Tu-160 in service

cyber.note: Anchor: cyber 9 = 1990 networks. Evidence: military computer networks limited; ES EVM mainframes, KGB SIGINT; behind the US

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID CSV) USSR 1989 = 11,336 (2011 int$); Russia alone 12,766 (high). Western estimates of Soviet output carry wide uncertainty (low).

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Soviet Military Power 1989: Western estimate 15-17 percent of GNP in the mid-1980s; Soviet official defence budget 77.3 billion rubles in 1989 (about 9% of GNP, low). COW milex 1989 = $119.4bn.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: industry ~40-45% of Soviet net material product in the late 1980s; heavy-industry economy.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of the labour force (share of food output not eaten by the farm population; no calorie self-sufficiency adjustment). CIA World Factbook 1990 (Project Gutenberg #14) labour force, Soviet Union: 20% agriculture (1989). World Bank WDI Database Archives (version 1999 Apr), SL.AGR.TOTL.ZS "Labor force in agriculture (% of total)" (ILO-based) Russia alone 1989 = 13.9% (low end of the share range 16%); high 23% for collective-farm under-reporting. The USSR imported grain heavily, but that does not lower this value. Share 20.0% (range 16.0-23.0%) -> 0.8 (0.77-0.84).

annualCohort.note: Educated guess: males reaching 18 in 1989 = males born 1971 (~4.6M USSR births, about 51% male) less mortality.

artillery.note: SMP 1989: towed field artillery 1,000, SP 900, MRLs 480 per year (1986-88 average).

armor.note: Soviet Military Power 1989 production tables: tanks 3,400 per year (1986-88 average), 3,300-3,500 in 1986-88; totals include exports.

ifv_apc.note: SMP 1989: other armoured vehicles 4,600 per year (1986-88 average), 4,200-5,250 by year.

aircraft_fighter.note: SMP 1989: fighters 680 per year 1986-88 (950 in 1982-84, high).

aircraft_strike.note: SMP 1989: bombers ~40-47 per year (OCR uncertain); fighter-bomber production is inside the fighter line; high allows wartime surge.

helicopters.note: SMP 1989: military helicopters 450 per year 1986-88 (580 in 1982-84).

ships_major.note: SMP 1989: surface warships 9 per year (1982-84 and 1986-88 averages).

ships_minor.note: SMP 1989: minor surface combatants 55 per year 1986-88.

missiles.note: Educated guess: launchers per year; SMP 1989 gives 116 ICBMs and ~520 SRBMs per year (missiles, not launchers).

air_defense.note: Educated guess: SAM batteries per year; SMP 1989 gives ~16,000 SAMs (missiles) per year.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: hard-surfaced roads ~1M km of ~1.6M km total in the late 1980s; poor rural roads.

railKm.note: Educated guess: common-carrier railways ~147,000 km in 1989 plus extensive industrial track; BAM completed 1984.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: Leningrad, Riga, Tallinn, Klaipeda, Odessa, Ilyichevsk, Novorossiysk, Murmansk, Arkhangelsk, Vladivostok, Nakhodka, Vostochny, Baku plus naval bases.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Soviet merchant fleet ~25M dwt in 1989 (Morflot), one of the largest in the world.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: Soviet front operations planned for 400-600 km depth with rail and truck brigades; reliance on railheads.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: horses ~5.9M in the late 1980s; militarily negligible.

nuclearWarheads.note: FAS estimate (Kristensen and Korda, via OWID nuclear-warhead-stockpiles CSV, listed under Russia) 1989 = 35,078 warheads; the Soviet stockpile peaked near 40,000 in 1986 (Norris and Kristensen).

basesAbroad.name: Wuensdorf (Western Group of Forces HQ), East Germany
Cam Ranh Bay naval base, Vietnam

homeDefense.note: 1.3 row: deep strategic depth, harsh winter climate and fortified cities (Russia anchor).

notes: Snapshot date mid-1989 (IISS Military Balance 1989-90 era), after the Afghanistan withdrawal (Feb 1989) and before the Eastern European revolutions; Gorbachev's unilateral cut of 500,000 men, 10,000 tanks, 8,500 artillery and 800 aircraft (announced Dec 1988) was under way. Population convention: all 15 union republics. Forces include the Western, Northern, Central and Southern Groups of Forces abroad (~550,000 men in Eastern Europe) and stored equipment east of the Urals. Key equipment totals from the DoD Soviet Military Power 1989 (archive.org full text) cross-checked against IISS Military Balance 1991-92 figures quoted in Wikipedia; personnel from COW NMC v7. Food: the USSR imported 25-40M t of grain per year in the 1980s; foodSurplus follows the SOURCES convention (positive, import dependence noted). KGB border troops (~230,000) and MVD troops (~340,000) are excluded from activePersonnel.
